title: Smith v. Kansas City Title & Trust Co. (1921)
summary: The shareholder action presented a substantial federal constitutional issue because the challenged investment depended on the validity of federal bonds.
notes:
The decision does not make every state claim containing any federal issue jurisdictionally federal. The later cases require necessity, actual dispute, substantiality to the federal system, and consistency with the federal-state division of judicial work.

Smith sued in the Western District of Missouri to enjoin the company from investing in farm-loan bonds issued under the Federal Farm Loan Act of 1916; Missouri law allowed the trust company to invest only in securities authorized by valid law, so the state-law claim turned on the Act's constitutionality, which the Court (Justice Day) then upheld on the merits.

sections.Parties: A shareholder sought to prevent a bank from investing in federal bonds alleged to have been issued under unconstitutional legislation.
sections.Material Facts: The shareholder’s asserted corporate-law entitlement arose under state law. The reason offered for prohibiting the investment, however, was that the federal legislation authorizing the bonds was unconstitutional. Resolving that constitutional challenge was necessary to deciding the claim as presented.
sections.Procedural History: The Supreme Court sustained federal jurisdiction over the action. The casebook places the decision alongside American Well Works and the later embedded-issue cases.
sections.Issue: Could federal-question jurisdiction exist although state law created the shareholder’s cause of action?
sections.Holding: Yes. The necessarily presented, important constitutional question supplied the federal character of this dispute.
sections.Reasoning: The validity of federal bonds had significance extending beyond the parties’ private disagreement. The federal issue was part of the shareholder’s own asserted basis for relief, not merely an anticipated response to a defense. Smith therefore illustrates the possibility of arising-under jurisdiction over a state-created claim. Grable and Gunn later state more explicit requirements limiting that category.

learning.why: The shareholder action presented a substantial federal constitutional issue because the challenged investment depended on the validity of federal bonds.

topics.cp-embedded-question: The shareholder’s state-law claim necessarily contested the constitutional validity of federal bonds.
topics.cp-federal-question: An important federal issue could support jurisdiction even where state law created the claim.
topics.cp-well-pleaded: The federal constitutional question appeared on the face of the plaintiff's own claim, which is why Smith satisfies the well-pleaded complaint rule while Mottley did not.
topics.cp-usc-1331: Smith is the classic example of § 1331 jurisdiction over a state-law claim that necessarily raises a substantial federal issue, later systematized in Grable.

learning.separateOpinions: Justice Holmes dissented, joined by Justice McReynolds, arguing that a suit arises under the law that creates the cause of action, which here was Missouri law.

mnemonic.rationale: Farm-loan bonds a trust company could not buy
